opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this comes out of the way we think about decomposing a network's parameters. In approaches like attribution-based or stochastic parameter decomposition, we try to write the network's weights as a sum of components, where each component ideally corresponds to one mechanism the network actually uses on its training distribution. The constraint is that the components have to add back up to the original weights.

Trained networks aren't clean. Training is a noisy process, and plenty ends up in the weights that doesn't contribute to the network's behavior on the data it sees. There's leftover structure from the random initialization that gradient descent never had a reason to remove. Some directions in parameter space get little or no gradient because no input in the training distribution activates them. There's also accumulated noise that roughly cancels out in practice. None of that is a mechanism in any meaningful sense, but it's still part of the weights.

Because of the faithfulness constraint, that stuff has to go somewhere in the decomposition. You don't want it smeared across your real mechanisms, because then each mechanism looks less simple and less interpretable than it really is. What tends to happen, and what we expect to happen, is that the optimization puts it into one component that's basically never causally important. You can ablate it on any input and the output barely changes. It isn't computing anything. It just absorbs the part of the parameters that the network doesn't use.

So I think of it as a feature of the method rather than a bug. It's evidence that the decomposition is separating "parameters the network uses" from "parameters that happen to be there." Without that component, you'd have to believe every scrap of weight-space structure is functional, and I don't think anyone who's looked at real trained networks believes that.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the junk component to unused parameters, leftover initialization, and noise, but does not explain it through parameter degeneracy where different parameter settings implement the same algorithm.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention ReLU units or the computation-preserving operation of scaling weights before a ReLU and inversely scaling weights after it.

fable-5.1.text:
Great question, and it comes directly out of the way we've been thinking about decomposing networks in our parameter decomposition work.

So the basic idea is that when you train a network with gradient descent, there's no pressure for every single parameter to be doing something useful. You have this enormous parameter space, and the loss only constrains the directions in that space that actually affect the outputs on the training distribution. Everything orthogonal to that is essentially free. Initialization puts a bunch of random stuff there, and if the gradients never push on it, it just stays. So you end up with this residue of weights that is, functionally speaking, doing nothing. It's there, it has nonzero values, but if you ablated it on the training distribution the behavior wouldn't change.

Now, the subtle thing is that this junk isn't necessarily sitting in a neat, separable place. It's mixed in with the parameters that are doing real work. So from the outside, if you just look at the weights, you can't easily tell the useful component from the useless one. But when you try to decompose the network into a set of mechanisms, where each mechanism is supposed to be responsible for some piece of the computation, you find that there's this leftover chunk that doesn't participate in any of them. It doesn't help predict any output on any input. It just accounts for some of the parameter mass.

And I think there are a couple of reasons to expect this to be really common rather than an edge case. One is overparameterization. Modern networks are much bigger than they need to be to represent the functions they end up learning, so there's a lot of slack. Two is that regularization is usually weak or indirect. Weight decay shrinks things, but it doesn't shrink them all the way to zero in finite training, and plenty of training setups barely use it. Three is that the random initialization has structure of its own, and some of that structure is just going to survive because it's never relevant to the loss.

The reason I think this matters for interpretability is that if you're trying to explain a network's behavior and you insist on explaining every parameter, you're going to waste a lot of effort trying to find a story for things that have no story. The honest answer for that component is "it does nothing." A good decomposition method should be able to say that. It should give you the mechanisms that matter, and then a separate bucket that it's willing to label as inert. If your method can't do that, it's probably going to smear the junk across the mechanisms and make them all look messier than they really are.

There's also a slightly deeper point, which is that "junk on the training distribution" doesn't mean "junk everywhere." Those parameters could matter off-distribution. So when I say it does nothing, I mean something fairly precise: it doesn't contribute to the network's behavior on the inputs it was trained on. That's exactly the kind of thing you'd want to flag from a safety perspective, because it's capacity that's unaccounted for by the normal story of what the model does.

r001.rationale: The response describes unconstrained parameter directions and weights that do not affect behavior on the training distribution, but does not explain the expectation through different parameter settings implementing exactly the same algorithm.

r002.rationale: It does not mention rescaling a weight before a ReLU and inversely rescaling a weight after it while preserving computation.

astra-6.text:
Well, the basic intuition is that the network has more degrees of freedom than it needs to implement its actual computation. Training constrains its behavior, but it doesn’t necessarily constrain every part of the weights. So you can have structure in the weights that doesn’t contribute to what the network does.

For example, two components might have effects that cancel each other out, or a component might lie in a direction that downstream layers ignore. And if that structure doesn’t affect the loss, there may be no pressure from gradient descent to remove it. Some of it could just be left over from initialization.

So when I say “junk,” I don’t necessarily mean a distinct set of neurons that are switched off. It could be mixed in with the useful structure. That matters for interpretability because explaining everything in the weights might be a different task from explaining the computation the network actually performs.

r001.rationale: The response says unused weight structure may remain because it does not affect the loss, and gives cancellation as an example. It does not clearly explain that distinct parameter settings can implement exactly the same algorithm.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention ReLU units or the computation-preserving operation of scaling the incoming weight up and the outgoing weight down.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, we usually train networks that have far more capacity than they need to solve a particular task. And we initialize them randomly. So training has to build the computations that help reduce the loss, but it doesn’t necessarily have to remove everything else. If some part of the network has no effect on the output, there’s no gradient telling it to go away.

So you can imagine the network containing a useful computation alongside a kind of leftover random computation. That leftover part might have activations and quite substantial weights, but its contributions cancel out or never reach the output. That’s what I mean by junk: it’s present in the parameters, but it isn’t doing anything functionally.

r001.rationale: The response attributes junk to excess capacity, random initialization, and lack of gradients removing functionally irrelevant parts. It does not explain parameter degeneracy as different parameter settings implementing the same algorithm.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe scaling a weight before a ReLU and inversely scaling a weight after it while preserving the computation.
